title: Rachel weeping (Jeremiah 31:14–16)
hookLine: Rachel weeps for her children, and is told "there is hope for thy future"
last: PLANT A GARDEN THERE, AND PRAY FOR THE PLACE.

lines: A VOICE WAS HEARD IN RAMAH.
cards: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel. Jacob's beloved, the wife he waited and worked for.
She died on the road, giving birth to a son, and Genesis says she was buried there, in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Generations later, Jeremiah hears her voice again.
Her children are being led away into exile, and she is weeping.

teach.b: Notice first what Rachel refuses: comfort. Not because comfort is bad, but because her children are gone, and nothing short of their return will do. The text lets her grief stand at full height.
Then God answers, and he doesn't tell her she's overreacting.
"Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Thy work.
Her weeping is called work, labor that will be paid. And then: "And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border."

teach.h: THERE IS HOPE FOR THY FUTURE.
teach.b: The Jewish Publication Society's old translation puts it this way: "there is hope for thy future." Rabbinic tradition built on this.

The commentator Rashi explains why Jacob buried Rachel on the road instead of in the family tomb: so that when her children were driven into exile, they would pass her grave, and she would come out and weep and plead for them.
And a midrash in Lamentations Rabbah tells that when the Temple fell, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses each pleaded for the people, and were not answered.
Then Rachel spoke, and God said: for your sake I will bring them back.
The one who refused comfort is the one whose tears are heard. Hope here isn't the opposite of grief. It's what God says to grief that refuses to quit.

how: These verses come near the end of the haftarah read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and people come to pray at the site known as Rachel's Tomb, near Bethlehem.

o: a prophet's wife lamenting the fallen Temple
a mother grieving her exiled children, and heard
a widow mourning her husband killed in battle

s: God tells Rachel her grief is too much
he calls her weeping work that shall be rewarded.
Genesis says Rachel was buried on the road to Ephrath
in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
in the midrash, Abraham's plea is the one answered
the ancestors and Moses plead without answer; Rachel's plea is answered.

games.q: you're Rachel, weeping for your children in exile. people come to comfort you. what do you do?
o: accept the comfort and stop crying.
refuse to be comforted, because they're gone.
tell them to forget the children.
games.why: she refused to be comforted for her children, and God answers her: there is hope, thy children shall come again.

practice: Let one person come to mind who seems far away right now, lost to addiction, to anger, to grief, to a life that's drifted from yours, and don't argue with how hard it is; Rachel didn't.
Let yourself care about them without pretending, and quietly set Jeremiah's words next to their name: there is hope. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Rachel weeping. The mother of the exiles, crying for her children and refusing comfort, and told: there is hope for thy future. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: there is hope, from Jeremiah 31:16 (JPS numbering).

carryVoice: Your line: there is hope. Her tears were called work, and they were heard. See you tomorrow.
